title: Kaliya
carry: spared, and sent to the ocean

segments.voice: Yesterday, Kaliya: the boy danced on the serpent's hoods until his pride was gone, and the serpent remembered the Lord. Did you meet an old habit with rhythm instead of a fight? Day eight hundred ninety-four.

The serpent is beaten. He lies broken in the water, and the boy is still standing on his heads. And now, out of the pool, come the serpent's wives. The Bhagavata calls them the naga wives, and they don't come to fight. They come with their children in front of them, their hair loose, their clothes disordered, and they bow down before Krishna with their palms joined. Kaliya can't speak for himself anymore. So they speak for him. Today belongs to the wives, and to what happens after a battle is won.
screen: `THE SERPENT IS BEATEN.` → `HIS WIVES COME OUT OF THE POOL.` → `THEY SPEAK FOR HIM.`

segments.voice: What the wives say is surprising. They don't argue that their husband is innocent. They say his punishment is fair. More than fair: they call it a grace. Your feet have touched his head, they say, and others perform long austerities hoping for the dust of those feet. Then they ask for one thing: spare him. He is our husband. Let him live. And Krishna lets him go. Kaliya, slowly, gets his breath back, and he speaks plainly. We serpents are born this way, he says. Angry by nature, with poison in us. It's hard to let go of what you're made of. Krishna doesn't lecture him. He gives him a way forward. Leave this pool, he says. Go to the ocean with your family, so the river can be clean again for the people and the cows. Then Krishna names the fear that brought Kaliya here in the first place. He was hiding. Garuda, the eagle who preys on serpents, could not enter this pool, because of a sage's old curse. So this poisoned corner of the Yamuna was the one place he felt safe. And Krishna answers that fear. Garuda won't harm you now, he says, because you carry the marks of my feet on your hoods. So the story ends without anyone destroyed. The poison leaves the river. The serpent leaves with his family, his fear answered. And the very feet that broke his pride become the thing that protects him.
screen: `"YOUR FEET HAVE TOUCHED HIS HEAD."` · `"WE ARE BORN THIS WAY."` · `GO TO THE OCEAN; LET THE RIVER BE CLEAN.` · then, large: `THE FOOTPRINTS PROTECT HIM.`

segments.voice: Sit, and let your shoulders drop. Bring to mind someone you struggle with, someone whose sharpness you've felt. Now, gently, wonder about one thing: what might they be afraid of? What corner did they crawl into to feel safe? You don't have to excuse anything. Just let that one question soften the picture a little as you breathe. Then, if you can, wish them somewhere better to live than their poison. If you pray, you can hold them in your prayer. The bell holds the time.
Kaliya. The serpent spared at his wives' plea, sent to the ocean, and protected by the very footprints that subdued him.
Your line: spared, and sent to the ocean. Today, when someone is sharp with you, ask quietly what they might be hiding from. Day eight hundred ninety-four.

howItsDone: Devotees retell the prayer of Kaliya's wives as a model of surrender, and in some depictions of Kaliya-mardana the naga wives are shown with joined palms beside the serpent.
